title: Hans mein Igel
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 108. Text from Wikisource („Hans mein Igel (1857)“, twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: KHM 108, one of the strangest of the collection's bridegroom tales. A farmer's angry wish for ‘a child, even if it's a hedgehog’ is granted literally: his son is born half boy, half hedgehog, is christened Hans My Hedgehog, and lies behind the stove for eight years before riding off — on a rooster shod like a horse, playing a bagpipe — to herd swine in the forest for years on end. Two kings, lost on the road, each promise him whatever first meets them at home in exchange for the way out; one tries to cheat him and sends his own daughter to be turned away bleeding and disgraced, the other keeps his word and gives Hans his daughter honestly. On the wedding night Hans has his hedgehog skin burned off by attendants standing ready at the fire, exactly as he has instructed, and emerges scorched black, then salved white and human by the king's own physician — a transformation as literal, and as un-gentle, as the wish that made him.

sentences.t: Es war einmal ein Bauer, der hatte Geld und Gut genung, aber wie reich er war, so fehlte doch etwas an seinem Glück:
sentences.l: There was once a peasant, he had money and goods enough, but however rich he was, yet something was lacking to his happiness:
sentences.i: There was once a farmer who had money and goods enough; but rich as he was, something was still wanting to his happiness:
sentences.n: “genung” is the 1857 form of “genug”, enough. “wie reich er war, so …” is a concession: however rich he was. “fehlen an” — to be lacking in.

sentences.t: er hatte mit seiner Frau keine Kinder.
sentences.l: he had no children with his wife.
sentences.n: German states it from the husband’s side; “keine Kinder haben mit” is the plain way of saying a couple was childless.

sentences.t: Öfters, wenn er mit den andern Bauern in die Stadt gieng, spotteten sie und fragten warum er keine Kinder hätte.
sentences.l: Often, when he went with the other farmers into the town, they mocked and asked why he had no children.
sentences.i: Often, when he went into town with the other farmers, they mocked him and asked why he had no children.
sentences.n: “Öfters” — time and again, repeatedly. “hätte” is subjunctive because the question is reported rather than quoted.

sentences.t: Da ward er endlich zornig, und als er nach Haus kam, sprach er „ich will ein Kind haben, und sollts ein Igel sein.“
sentences.l: Then became he at last angry, and when he came home, he spoke “I will have a child, and should it be a hedgehog.”
sentences.i: At last he grew angry, and when he came home he said, “I will have a child, even if it should be a hedgehog.”
sentences.n: “und sollts ein Igel sein” puts the verb first to make a concession: even if it were to be a hedgehog. “sollts” is “sollt es” run together. The whole tale hangs on this one rash word.

sentences.t: Da kriegte seine Frau ein Kind, das war oben ein Igel und unten ein Junge,
sentences.l: Then got his wife a child, that was above a hedgehog and below a boy,
sentences.i: Then his wife had a child that was a hedgehog above and a boy below,
sentences.n: “kriegen” — to get; the everyday word for having a child. German says “das war”, that was, where English wants a relative pronoun.

sentences.t: und als sie das Kind sah, erschrack sie und sprach „siehst du, du hast uns verwünscht.“
sentences.l: and when she saw the child, she took fright and spoke “you see, you have cursed us.”
sentences.i: and when she saw the child she took fright and said, “You see — you have wished a curse on us.”
sentences.n: “erschrack” is the older strong preterite of “erschrecken” (modern erschrak). “verwünschen” — to lay a wish upon, to curse: the husband’s angry word counts as a spell.

sentences.t: Da sprach der Mann „was kann das alles helfen, getauft muß der Junge werden, aber wir können keinen Gevatter dazu nehmen.“
sentences.l: Then spoke the man “what can all that help, baptized must the boy be, but we can take no godfather for it.”
sentences.i: Then the man said, “What good is any of that? The boy must be baptized, but we can get no godfather for him.”
sentences.n: “Gevatter” is the old word for a godfather (modern Pate); refusing to stand godfather to such a child is a real disgrace in village terms. “was kann das alles helfen” — what use is any of it.

sentences.t: Die Frau sprach „wir können ihn auch nicht anders taufen als Hans mein Igel.“
sentences.l: The wife spoke “we can also not baptize him otherwise than Hans my Hedgehog.”
sentences.i: The wife said, “And we cannot christen him anything but Hans My Hedgehog.”
sentences.n: “nicht anders … als” — no otherwise than, nothing but. The name keeps its possessive shape and is never inflected: he is “Hans mein Igel” in every case throughout the tale.

sentences.t: Als er getauft war, sagte der Pfarrer „der kann wegen seiner Stacheln in kein ordentlich Bett kommen.“
sentences.l: When he was baptized, the parson said “he cannot come into any proper bed because of his spines.”
sentences.i: When he had been baptized the parson said, “He cannot go into a proper bed, because of his spines.”
sentences.n: “der” at the head of the sentence is the demonstrative doing duty for “he”, as speech often does. “ordentlich” stands uninflected before “Bett”, ordinary enough in older written German.

sentences.t: Da ward hinter dem Ofen ein wenig Stroh zurecht gemacht und Hans mein Igel darauf gelegt.
sentences.l: Then was behind the stove a little straw made ready and Hans my Hedgehog laid upon it.
sentences.i: So a little straw was made ready behind the stove, and Hans My Hedgehog was laid on it.
sentences.n: The space behind the tiled stove is the warmest corner of a peasant house — and the place for whatever is to be kept out of the way. “zurecht machen” — to put right, prepare.

sentences.t: Er konnte auch an der Mutter nicht trinken, denn er hätte sie mit seinen Stacheln gestochen.
sentences.l: He could also not drink at the mother, for he would have pricked her with his spines.
sentences.i: Nor could he nurse at his mother, for he would have pricked her with his spines.
sentences.n: “an der Mutter trinken” — to drink at the mother, that is, to nurse. “hätte … gestochen” is the subjunctive of consequence: he would have.

sentences.t: So lag er da hinter dem Ofen acht Jahre, und sein Vater war ihn müde und dachte wenn er nur stürbe;
sentences.l: So lay he there behind the stove eight years, and his father was weary of him and thought if only he would die;
sentences.i: So he lay there behind the stove for eight years, and his father grew weary of him and thought, if only he would die;
sentences.n: “jemanden müde sein” — to be tired of someone, an older construction taking the accusative. “stürbe” is the subjunctive of “sterben”, and it carries the wish. “acht” here is the number eight, not the “Acht” of “in Acht nehmen”.

sentences.t: aber er starb nicht, sondern blieb da liegen.
sentences.l: but he did not die, but rather stayed lying there.
sentences.i: but he did not die; he went on lying there.
sentences.n: “sondern” contradicts something already denied — not this, but rather that. “blieb … liegen” — remained lying.

sentences.t: Nun trug es sich zu, daß in der Stadt ein Markt war, und der Bauer wollte hin gehen, da fragte er seine Frau, was er ihr sollte mitbringen.
sentences.l: Now it came about that in the town there was a market, and the farmer wanted to go there, so asked he his wife what he should bring back for her.
sentences.i: Now it came about that there was a market in the town, and the farmer meant to go; so he asked his wife what he should bring her back.
sentences.n: “es trug sich zu” — it came to pass (sich zutragen, separable). “mitbringen” — to bring along, bring back.

sentences.t: „Ein wenig Fleisch und ein paar Wecke, was zum Haushalt gehört“ sprach sie.
sentences.l: “A little meat and a couple of rolls, what belongs to the household,” spoke she.
sentences.i: “A little meat and a few white rolls — what a household needs,” said she.
sentences.n: “Wecke” are wheaten rolls. “was zum Haushalt gehört” — whatever belongs to the housekeeping. The 1857 text sets no comma before “sprach sie”.

sentences.t: Darauf fragte er die Magd, die wollte ein paar Toffeln und Zwickelstrümpfe.
sentences.l: Thereupon asked he the maid, she wanted a pair of slippers and gusset-stockings.
sentences.i: Then he asked the maidservant; she wanted a pair of slippers and gusseted stockings.
sentences.n: “Toffeln” is the colloquial short form of “Pantoffeln”, slippers. “Zwickelstrümpfe” are stockings with a “Zwickel”, the wedge-shaped gusset at the ankle — a small piece of finery.

sentences.t: Endlich sagte er auch „Hans mein Igel, was willst du denn haben?“
sentences.l: At last said he also “Hans my Hedgehog, what do you want then?”
sentences.i: At last he said too, “Hans My Hedgehog, and what will you have?”
sentences.n: “denn” inside a question is a flavouring word: it makes the question conversational rather than adding “then”.

sentences.t: „Väterchen,“ sprach er, „bring mir doch einen Dudelsack mit.“
sentences.l: “Little-father,” spoke he, “bring me but a bagpipe along.”
sentences.i: “Little father,” he said, “do bring me back a bagpipe.”
sentences.n: “Väterchen” is the diminutive of Vater, and the only tenderness in the son’s dealings with his father. “doch” in a request coaxes: do bring. “mitbringen” splits: “bring … mit”.

sentences.t: Wie nun der Bauer wieder nach Haus kam, gab er der Frau, was er ihr gekauft hatte, Fleisch und Wecke,
sentences.l: When now the farmer came home again, gave he the wife what he had bought her, meat and rolls,
sentences.i: When the farmer came home again he gave his wife what he had bought her, meat and rolls,
sentences.n: “der Frau” — the bare article does the work of a possessive; German often says “die Frau, der Mann” where English wants “his wife, her husband”.

sentences.t: dann gab er der Magd die Toffeln und die Zwickelstrümpfe,
sentences.l: then gave he the maid the slippers and the gusset-stockings,
sentences.i: then he gave the maid the slippers and the gusseted stockings,
sentences.n: “der Magd” is dative and “die Toffeln” accusative — the person given to comes first, exactly as in English “gave the maid the slippers”.

sentences.t: endlich gieng er hinter den Ofen und gab dem Hans mein Igel den Dudelsack.
sentences.l: at last went he behind the stove and gave to the Hans my Hedgehog the bagpipe.
sentences.i: and last of all he went behind the stove and gave Hans My Hedgehog the bagpipe.
sentences.n: “dem Hans mein Igel” puts the article in front of the whole name to mark the dative, while the name itself stays untouched.

sentences.t: Und wie Hans mein Igel den Dudelsack hatte, sprach er „Väterchen, geht doch vor die Schmiede und laßt mir meinen Göckelhahn beschlagen,
sentences.l: And when Hans my Hedgehog had the bagpipe, spoke he “Little-father, go to the smithy and have my cockerel shod for me,
sentences.i: And when Hans My Hedgehog had the bagpipe he said, “Little father, go to the smithy and have my cockerel shod,
sentences.n: The son addresses his father in the plural — “geht … laßt” — the respectful form children used to their parents. “Göckelhahn” is a dialect word for a cock. “beschlagen lassen” — to have shod, as one has a horse shod.

sentences.t: dann will ich fortreiten und will nimmermehr wiederkommen.“
sentences.l: then will I ride away and will nevermore come again.”
sentences.i: then I will ride away and never come back again.”
sentences.n: “nimmermehr” — nevermore; archaic in modern German, but plain speech in Grimm.

sentences.t: Da war der Vater froh daß er ihn los werden sollte,
sentences.l: Then was the father glad that he should be rid of him,
sentences.i: The father was glad that he should be rid of him,
sentences.n: “los werden” — to get rid of. The father’s relief is stated flatly, and the tale never softens it.

sentences.t: und ließ ihm den Hahn beschlagen, und als er fertig war, setzte sich Hans mein Igel darauf, ritt fort,
sentences.l: and had him the cock shod, and when it was ready, set himself Hans my Hedgehog upon it, rode away,
sentences.i: and had the cock shod for him; and when that was done Hans My Hedgehog seated himself upon it and rode away,
sentences.n: “ließ … beschlagen” — had it shod; “lassen” with an infinitive is “to have something done”. “ihm” is the dative of interest: for him.

sentences.t: nahm auch Schweine und Esel mit, die wollt er draußen im Walde hüten.
sentences.l: took also pigs and asses along, those he wanted to tend outside in the forest.
sentences.i: and took pigs and asses along with him, which he meant to tend out in the forest.
sentences.n: “mitnehmen” splits: “nahm … mit”. “wollt” is clipped “wollte”; “Walde” keeps the old dative -e.

sentences.t: Im Wald aber mußte der Hahn mit ihm auf einen hohen Baum fliegen,
sentences.l: In the forest however had the cock to fly with him up onto a high tree,
sentences.i: But in the forest the cock had to fly up into a tall tree with him,
sentences.n: “auf einen hohen Baum” with the accusative marks motion up onto the tree, not rest upon it.

sentences.t: da saß er und hütete die Esel und Schweine, und saß lange Jahre bis die Heerde ganz groß war,
sentences.l: there sat he and tended the asses and pigs, and sat long years until the herd was quite big,
sentences.i: there he sat and tended the asses and pigs, and sat for long years until the herd was very large,
sentences.n: “Heerde” is the 1857 spelling of Herde, herd.

sentences.t: und wußte sein Vater nichts von ihm.
sentences.l: and knew his father nothing of him.
sentences.i: and his father knew nothing of him.
sentences.n: The verb comes first because the clause hangs on the “und” before it: German keeps the run going where English would start a new sentence.

sentences.t: Wenn er aber auf dem Baum saß, blies er seinen Dudelsack und machte Musik, die war sehr schön.
sentences.l: But when he sat on the tree, blew he his bagpipe and made music, it was very beautiful.
sentences.i: But when he sat in the tree he blew his bagpipe and made music, and it was very beautiful.
sentences.n: “die war sehr schön” tacks a demonstrative on at the end instead of a relative clause — the plain spoken way of adding a remark.

sentences.t: Einmal kam ein König vorbeigefahren, der hatte sich verirrt, und hörte die Musik:
sentences.l: Once came a king driving past, he had lost his way, and heard the music:
sentences.i: Once a king came driving past who had lost his way, and he heard the music:
sentences.n: “sich verirren” — to go astray, lose one’s way. “kam … vorbeigefahren” pairs “come” with a participle: came driving past.

sentences.t: da verwunderte er sich darüber und schickte seinen Bedienten hin, er sollte sich einmal umgucken wo die Musik herkäme.
sentences.l: then wondered he at it and sent his servant thither, he should look around once where the music came from.
sentences.i: he wondered at it, and sent his servant over to look about and see where the music came from.
sentences.n: “sich verwundern über” — to marvel at. “herkäme” is subjunctive in the reported question; “herkommen” — to come from.

sentences.t: Er guckte sich um, sah aber nichts als ein kleines Thier auf dem Baum oben sitzen,
sentences.l: He looked around, saw however nothing but a little animal sitting up on the tree,
sentences.i: He looked about him, but saw nothing except a little creature sitting up in the tree,
sentences.n: “nichts als” — nothing but. “sich umgucken” — to look around (separable, a homelier word than umsehen).

sentences.t: das war wie ein Göckelhahn, auf dem ein Igel saß, und der machte die Musik.
sentences.l: that was like a cockerel, on which a hedgehog sat, and he made the music.
sentences.i: which was like a cockerel with a hedgehog sitting on it, and it was the hedgehog that made the music.
sentences.n: Three loose clauses in a row where English wants one sentence; the “der” at the end points back to the hedgehog, not to the cock.

sentences.t: Da sprach der König zum Bedienten er sollte fragen warum er da säße, und ob er nicht wüßte wo der Weg in sein Königreich gienge.
sentences.l: Then spoke the king to the servant he should ask why he was sitting there, and whether he did not know where the way into his kingdom went.
sentences.i: Then the king told the servant to ask why he was sitting there, and whether he did not know where the road into his kingdom ran.
sentences.n: Reported speech without “daß”: the verbs go into the subjunctive instead — “säße”, “wüßte”, “gienge”. This is how Grimm reports what was said, and it runs through the whole tale.

sentences.t: Da stieg Hans mein Igel vom Baum und sprach er wollte den Weg zeigen,
sentences.l: Then climbed Hans my Hedgehog down from the tree and said he would show the way,
sentences.i: Then Hans My Hedgehog climbed down from the tree and said that he would show the way,
sentences.n: “wollte” in reported speech is the subjunctive of “wollen”: he was willing to.

sentences.t: wenn der König ihm wollte verschreiben und versprechen was ihm zuerst begegnete am königlichen Hofe, sobald er nach Haus käme.
sentences.l: if the king would make over to him in writing and promise what met him first at the royal court, as soon as he came home.
sentences.i: if the king would sign over to him and promise him whatever should first meet him at the royal court as soon as he came home.
sentences.n: “verschreiben” — to make over by written deed; the rash promise is a legal act, which is why a paper has to be drawn up. The bargain of “whatever meets you first” is an old trap in folktale, and what meets the promiser first is always his own child.

sentences.t: Da dachte der König „das kann ich leicht thun, Hans mein Igel verstehts doch nicht, und ich kann schreiben was ich will.“
sentences.l: Then thought the king “that can I easily do, Hans my Hedgehog does not understand it anyway, and I can write what I want.”
sentences.i: Then the king thought, “I can easily do that; Hans My Hedgehog does not understand it in any case, and I can write whatever I like.”
sentences.n: “verstehts” is “versteht es” run together. “doch” here means “after all, anyway”. “thun” is the 1857 spelling of tun.

sentences.t: Da nahm der König Feder und Dinte und schrieb etwas auf,
sentences.l: Then took the king quill and ink and wrote something down,
sentences.i: Then the king took pen and ink and wrote something down,
sentences.n: “Dinte” is the older spelling of “Tinte”, ink. “aufschreiben” splits: “schrieb … auf”. “Feder” is the quill, the pen — the writing sense of the word, not a feather.

sentences.t: und als es geschehen war, zeigte ihm Hans mein Igel den Weg, und er kam glücklich nach Haus.
sentences.l: and when it had happened, showed him Hans my Hedgehog the way, and he came safely home.
sentences.i: and when that was done Hans My Hedgehog showed him the way, and he came safely home.
sentences.n: “glücklich” in older usage means safely, successfully — not in a happy frame of mind.

sentences.t: Seine Tochter aber, wie sie ihn von weitem sah, war so voll Freuden, daß sie ihm entgegen lief und ihn küßte.
sentences.l: His daughter however, when she saw him from afar, was so full of joys that she ran toward him and kissed him.
sentences.i: But his daughter, when she saw him from afar, was so full of joy that she ran to meet him and kissed him.
sentences.n: “voll Freuden” keeps the old genitive plural after “voll”. “entgegen laufen” — to run to meet, with the person in the dative (“ihm”).

sentences.t: Da gedachte er an Hans mein Igel und erzählte ihr wie es ihm gegangen wäre,
sentences.l: Then thought he of Hans my Hedgehog and told her how it had gone with him,
sentences.i: Then he remembered Hans My Hedgehog and told her how things had gone with him,
sentences.n: “gedenken an” — to call to mind. “wie es ihm gegangen wäre” is impersonal: how it had gone *for* him; the subjunctive marks it as reported.

sentences.t: und daß er einem wunderlichen Thier hätte verschreiben sollen was ihm daheim zuerst begegnen würde,
sentences.l: and that he had had to make over to a strange animal whatever would meet him first at home,
sentences.i: and that he had had to sign over to a strange creature whatever should first meet him at home,
sentences.n: “wunderlich” — strange, odd; not “wonderful”. “hätte verschreiben sollen” piles three verbs at the end, the order German requires when a modal goes into the perfect.

sentences.t: und das Thier hätte auf einem Hahn wie auf einem Pferde gesessen und schöne Musik gemacht;
sentences.l: and the animal had sat upon a cock as upon a horse and made beautiful music;
sentences.i: and that the creature had sat on a cock as though on a horse and made beautiful music;
sentences.n: “Pferde” keeps the old dative -e. The subjunctive “hätte … gesessen” carries the king’s report on.

sentences.t: er hätte aber geschrieben es sollts nicht haben, denn Hans mein Igel könnt es doch nicht lesen.
sentences.l: he had however written it should not have it, for Hans my Hedgehog could not read it anyway.
sentences.i: but that he had written that it should not have her, for Hans My Hedgehog could not read it in any case.
sentences.n: “es sollts nicht haben”: the first “es” is the creature, and the “-s” stuck onto “sollts” is what was promised — which is the daughter herself. The idiomatic line says “her”, which is what the German means without saying it.

sentences.t: Darüber war die Prinzessin froh und sagte das wäre gut, denn sie wäre doch nimmermehr hingegangen.
sentences.l: At that was the princess glad and said that would be good, for she would never have gone there anyway.
sentences.i: The princess was glad at that, and said it was just as well, for she would never have gone to him in any case.
sentences.n: “hingehen” — to go there. The subjunctives “wäre” keep the words hers rather than the narrator’s.

sentences.t: Hans mein Igel aber hütete die Esel und Schweine, war immer lustig, saß auf dem Baum und blies auf seinem Dudelsack.
sentences.l: Hans my Hedgehog however tended the asses and pigs, was always merry, sat on the tree and blew upon his bagpipe.
sentences.i: But Hans My Hedgehog tended his asses and pigs, was always merry, and sat in his tree blowing his bagpipe.
sentences.n: “lustig” — merry, in good spirits; not “funny”.

sentences.t: Nun geschah es, daß ein anderer König gefahren kam mit seinen Bedienten und Laufern,
sentences.l: Now it happened that another king came driving with his servants and runners,
sentences.i: Now it happened that another king came driving by with his servants and running footmen,
sentences.n: “Laufer” (modern Läufer) are the footmen who ran ahead of a great man’s carriage — a fixture of the old courts.

sentences.t: und hatte sich verirrt, und wußte nicht wieder nach Haus zu kommen, weil der Wald so groß war.
sentences.l: and had lost his way, and did not know to come home again, because the forest was so big.
sentences.i: and had lost his way, and did not know how to get home again, the forest being so vast.
sentences.n: “wußte nicht … zu kommen” — did not know how to get there; German leaves the “how” out and lets the infinitive with “zu” carry it.

sentences.t: Da hörte er gleichfalls die schöne Musik von weitem und sprach zu seinem Laufer was das wohl wäre, er sollte einmal zusehen.
sentences.l: Then heard he likewise the beautiful music from afar and spoke to his runner what that might be, he should once go and see.
sentences.i: He too heard the beautiful music from afar, and said to his footman, whatever could that be — he should go and see.
sentences.n: “was das wohl wäre”: “wohl” turns it into a wondering question, what on earth that might be. “zusehen” — to go and look on.

sentences.t: Da gieng der Laufer hin unter den Baum und sah den Göckelhahn sitzen und Hans mein Igel oben drauf.
sentences.l: Then went the runner over under the tree and saw the cockerel sitting and Hans my Hedgehog on top of it.
sentences.i: So the footman went over beneath the tree and saw the cockerel sitting there with Hans My Hedgehog on top.
sentences.n: “drauf” is the spoken contraction of “darauf”, on it.

sentences.t: Der Laufer fragte ihn was er da oben vorhätte.
sentences.l: The runner asked him what he had in mind up there.
sentences.i: The footman asked him what he was about up there.
sentences.n: “vorhaben” — to have in mind, to be up to; separable, and here in the subjunctive “vorhätte” of reported speech.

sentences.t: „Ich hüte meine Esel und Schweine; aber was ist euer Begehren?“
sentences.l: “I tend my asses and pigs; but what is your desire?”
sentences.i: “I am tending my asses and pigs — but what is it you want?”
sentences.n: “euer” is the plural “your”, the polite address of the day. “Begehren” — desire, request: a formal word, and the hedgehog uses it with a certain dignity. “hüte” is the 1st sg. present, I tend — not the imperative of “sich hüten”, to beware.

sentences.t: Der Laufer sagte sie hätten sich verirrt und könnten nicht wieder ins Königreich, ob er ihnen den Weg nicht zeigen wollte.
sentences.l: The runner said they had lost their way and could not again into the kingdom, whether he would not show them the way.
sentences.i: The footman said they had lost their way and could not get back to their kingdom, and would he not show them the road.
sentences.n: “könnten nicht wieder ins Königreich” leaves the verb of motion out: could not [get] back into the kingdom. The subjunctives again mark reported speech.

sentences.t: Da stieg Hans mein Igel mit dem Hahn vom Baum herunter,
sentences.l: Then climbed Hans my Hedgehog with the cock down from the tree,
sentences.i: Then Hans My Hedgehog climbed down from the tree with the cock,
sentences.n: “herunter steigen” — to climb down; the particle “herunter” marks motion downwards and towards the speaker.

sentences.t: und sagte zu dem alten König er wolle ihm den Weg zeigen,
sentences.l: and said to the old king he would show him the way,
sentences.n: “wolle” is the subjunctive I of “wollen”, the form used for reporting a person’s own words.

sentences.t: wenn er ihm zu eigen geben wollte was ihm zu Haus vor seinem königlichen Schlosse das erste begegnen würde.
sentences.l: if he would give him as his own what would meet him first at home before his royal castle.
sentences.i: if he would give over to him as his own whatever should first meet him at home before his royal castle.
sentences.n: “zu eigen geben” — to give as property, to make over. The second king is asked for exactly the bargain the first was asked for; the difference is that this one keeps it.

sentences.t: Der König sagte „ja,“ und unterschrieb sich dem Hans mein Igel, er sollte es haben.
sentences.l: The king said “yes,” and signed himself to Hans my Hedgehog, he should have it.
sentences.i: The king said yes, and put his name to a bond for Hans My Hedgehog that he should have it.
sentences.n: “sich unterschreiben” — to put one’s name to a bond, to bind oneself in writing; the reflexive makes the king himself the thing bound.

sentences.t: Als das geschehen war, ritt er auf dem Göckelhahn voraus und zeigte ihm den Weg, und gelangte der König glücklich wieder in sein Reich.
sentences.l: When that had happened, rode he ahead upon the cockerel and showed him the way, and got the king safely back into his realm.
sentences.i: When that was done he rode ahead on the cockerel and showed him the way, and the king came safely back to his realm.
sentences.n: “voraus reiten” — to ride on ahead. “gelangen” — to arrive, to get to; “glücklich” once more in its old sense of safely.

sentences.t: Wie er auf den Hof kam, war große Freude darüber.
sentences.l: When he came into the courtyard, was there great joy over it.
sentences.i: When he came into the courtyard there was great rejoicing over it.
sentences.n: “Hof” is both the courtyard and the court; here it is the palace yard.

sentences.t: Nun hatte er eine einzige Tochter, die war sehr schön,
sentences.l: Now had he one only daughter, she was very beautiful,
sentences.i: Now he had an only daughter, and she was very beautiful,
sentences.n: “einzig” — sole, only. The demonstrative “die” again does the work of a relative pronoun.

sentences.t: die lief ihm entgegen, fiel ihm um den Hals und küßte ihn und freute sich daß ihr alter Vater wieder kam.
sentences.l: she ran to meet him, fell about his neck and kissed him and rejoiced that her old father came again.
sentences.i: she ran to meet him, threw her arms about his neck and kissed him, and rejoiced that her old father had come back.
sentences.n: “jemandem um den Hals fallen” — to fall about someone’s neck, to embrace them; the one embraced stands in the dative.

sentences.t: Sie fragte ihn auch wo er so lange in der Welt gewesen wäre,
sentences.l: She asked him also where he had been so long in the world,
sentences.i: She asked him too where in the world he had been all that time,
sentences.n: “in der Welt” inside the question is the same intensifier as the English “where in the world”.

sentences.t: da erzählte er ihr er hätte sich verirrt und wäre beinahe gar nicht wieder gekommen,
sentences.l: then told he her he had lost his way and had almost not come back at all,
sentences.i: so he told her that he had lost his way and had almost not come back at all,
sentences.n: “beinahe” — almost; “gar nicht” — not at all.

sentences.t: aber als er durch einen großen Wald gefahren wäre, hätte einer, halb wie ein Igel, halb wie ein Mensch, rittlings auf einem Hahn in einem hohen Baum gesessen, und schöne Musik gemacht,
sentences.l: but as he had driven through a great forest, someone had sat, half like a hedgehog, half like a man, astride upon a cock in a high tree, and made beautiful music,
sentences.i: but that as he was driving through a great forest, someone half hedgehog and half man had been sitting astride a cock in a tall tree, making beautiful music,
sentences.n: “rittlings” — astride. “einer” is the indefinite “someone”: the king’s account holds the creature at arm’s length, calling it neither man nor beast.

sentences.t: der hätte ihm fortgeholfen und den Weg gezeigt,
sentences.l: he had helped him on and shown the way,
sentences.i: and that he had helped him on his way and shown him the road,
sentences.n: “forthelfen” — to help someone on, help them get away (separable, with the person helped in the dative).

sentences.t: er aber hätte ihm dafür versprochen was ihm am königlichen Hofe zuerst begegnete, und das wäre sie,
sentences.l: he however had promised him for that what met him first at the royal court, and that was she,
sentences.i: but that in return he had promised him whatever should first meet him at the royal court — and that was she,
sentences.n: “und das wäre sie”: the subjunctive keeps the sentence inside the king’s own telling, and German uses the nominative “sie” after “sein”.

sentences.t: und das thäte ihm nun so leid.
sentences.l: and that grieved him now so much.
sentences.i: and now he was so sorry for it.
sentences.n: “es thut mir leid” — I am sorry, literally “it does me sorrow”; “thäte” is the subjunctive, the 1857 spelling of täte.

sentences.t: Da versprach sie ihm aber sie wollte gerne mit ihm gehen wann er käme, ihrem alten Vater zu Liebe.
sentences.l: But then promised she him she would gladly go with him when he came, for love of her old father.
sentences.i: But she promised him that she would gladly go with him when he came, for her old father’s sake.
sentences.n: “jemandem zu Liebe” — for someone’s sake, out of love for them (modern: zuliebe). “wann” stands here for “wenn”, when.

sentences.t: Hans mein Igel aber hütete seine Schweine, und die Schweine bekamen wieder Schweine, und wurden ihrer so viel, daß der ganze Wald voll war.
sentences.l: Hans my Hedgehog however tended his pigs, and the pigs got pigs again, and there became so many of them that the whole forest was full.
sentences.i: Meanwhile Hans My Hedgehog tended his pigs, and the pigs had pigs again, and there came to be so many of them that the whole forest was full.
sentences.n: “wurden ihrer so viel” — there became so many of them, with the old genitive “ihrer”, of them.

sentences.t: Da wollte Hans mein Igel nicht länger im Walde leben, und ließ seinem Vater sagen sie sollten alle Ställe im Dorf räumen,
sentences.l: Then wanted Hans my Hedgehog no longer to live in the forest, and let it be said to his father they should clear all the stalls in the village,
sentences.i: Then Hans My Hedgehog no longer wished to live in the forest, and sent word to his father that they should clear every stall in the village,
sentences.n: “ließ seinem Vater sagen” — had it said to his father, that is, sent word; “lassen” with an infinitive again.

sentences.t: denn er käme mit einer so großen Heerde, daß jeder schlachten könnte, der nur schlachten wollte.
sentences.l: for he was coming with so great a herd that everyone could slaughter who only wanted to slaughter.
sentences.i: for he was coming with so great a herd that anyone who wished to slaughter might slaughter.
sentences.n: “der nur schlachten wollte” — whoever might wish to; “nur” after a relative gives it the force of “-ever”.

sentences.t: Da war sein Vater betrübt, als er das hörte, denn er dachte Hans mein Igel wäre schon lange gestorben.
sentences.l: Then was his father troubled when he heard that, for he thought Hans my Hedgehog had died long ago.
sentences.i: His father was troubled when he heard it, for he thought Hans My Hedgehog had died long since.
sentences.n: “betrübt” — grieved, cast down. What grieves the father is the son’s return, not his death.

sentences.t: Hans mein Igel aber setzte sich auf seinen Göckelhahn, trieb die Schweine vor sich her ins Dorf, und ließ schlachten;
sentences.l: Hans my Hedgehog however set himself upon his cockerel, drove the pigs before him into the village, and had them slaughtered;
sentences.i: But Hans My Hedgehog seated himself on his cockerel, drove the pigs before him into the village, and had the slaughtering done;
sentences.n: “vor sich her treiben” — to drive along in front of oneself. “ließ schlachten” leaves the object out: had [them] slaughtered.

sentences.t: hu! da war ein Gemetzel und ein Hacken, daß mans zwei Stunden weit hören konnte.
sentences.l: hu! there was a butchery and a hacking, so that one could hear it two hours far.
sentences.i: Hu! There was such a butchering and hacking that it could be heard two hours’ distance away.
sentences.n: “hu!” is the narrator’s own shudder, dropped into the sentence — the same interjection that stands, more strangely, mid-sentence in KHM 102. “zwei Stunden weit” measures distance by walking time, as country speech does. “mans” is “man es”. “ein Hacken” is the infinitive used as a noun: a hacking.

sentences.t: Danach sagte Hans mein Igel „Väterchen, laßt mir meinen Göckelhahn noch einmal vor der Schmiede beschlagen, dann reit ich fort und komme mein Lebtag nicht wieder.“
sentences.l: After that said Hans my Hedgehog “Little-father, have my cockerel shod once more before the smithy, then ride I away and come not again all my days.”
sentences.i: After that Hans My Hedgehog said, “Little father, have my cockerel shod once more at the smithy; then I shall ride away and never come back as long as I live.”
sentences.n: “mein Lebtag” — all my days, as long as I live (an old accusative of time). The respectful plural “laßt” to the father again.

sentences.t: Da ließ der Vater den Göckelhahn beschlagen und war froh daß Hans mein Igel nicht wieder kommen wollte.
sentences.l: Then had the father the cockerel shod and was glad that Hans my Hedgehog did not want to come again.
sentences.i: So the father had the cockerel shod, and was glad that Hans My Hedgehog did not mean to come back.
sentences.n: The father’s gladness at losing him is stated twice in the tale, and the narrator never once comments on it.

sentences.t: Hans mein Igel ritt fort in das erste Königreich,
sentences.l: Hans my Hedgehog rode away into the first kingdom,
sentences.n: “das erste Königreich” — the first of the two, whose king had written a false bond.

sentences.t: da hatte der König befohlen wenn einer käme auf einem Hahn geritten, und hätte einen Dudelsack bei sich,
sentences.l: there had the king commanded, if anyone came riding upon a cock, and had a bagpipe with him,
sentences.i: there the king had given orders that if anyone came riding on a cock and had a bagpipe with him,
sentences.n: “käme … geritten” — should come riding; the subjunctive belongs to the reported order.

sentences.t: dann sollten alle auf ihn schießen, hauen und stechen, damit er nicht ins Schloß käme.
sentences.l: then should all shoot at him, hack and stab, so that he might not get into the castle.
sentences.i: then everyone should shoot at him, hack and stab, so that he should not get into the castle.
sentences.n: “damit” — so that, in order that; it takes an ordinary clause with the verb at the end.

sentences.t: Als nun Hans mein Igel daher geritten kam, drangen sie mit den Bajonetten auf ihn ein,
sentences.l: When now Hans my Hedgehog came riding up, pressed they in on him with the bayonets,
sentences.i: So when Hans My Hedgehog came riding up, they set upon him with their bayonets,
sentences.n: “auf jemanden eindringen” — to press in on, to assail (separable: drangen … ein). Bayonets in a fairy tale are one of the newer touches the Grimms let stand.

sentences.t: aber er gab dem Hahn die Sporn, flog auf, über das Thor hin vor des Königs Fenster, ließ sich da nieder,
sentences.l: but he gave the cock the spur, flew up, away over the gate before the king’s window, set himself down there,
sentences.i: but he set spurs to the cock, flew up and away over the gate to the king’s window, and settled there,
sentences.n: “die Sporn geben” — to give the spur, set spurs to. “sich nieder lassen” — to set oneself down, to alight. “Thor” is the 1857 spelling of Tor, gate.

sentences.t: und rief ihm zu er sollt ihm geben was er versprochen hätte,
sentences.l: and called to him he should give him what he had promised,
sentences.i: and called to him that he must give him what he had promised,
sentences.n: “sollt” is clipped “sollte”. Two datives stand side by side in “ihm … ihm”: the first is the king, the second the hedgehog.

sentences.t: sonst so wollt er ihm und seiner Tochter das Leben nehmen.
sentences.l: otherwise so would he take from him and from his daughter the life.
sentences.i: or else he would take the life of both him and his daughter.
sentences.n: “sonst so” doubles the connective, as spoken German does. “jemandem das Leben nehmen” — to take someone’s life, with the person in the dative.

sentences.t: Da gab der König seiner Tochter gute Worte, sie möchte zu ihm hinaus gehen, damit sie ihm und sich das Leben rettete.
sentences.l: Then gave the king his daughter good words, she might go out to him, so that she should save his life and her own.
sentences.i: Then the king coaxed his daughter with fair words to go out to him, so that she might save his life and her own.
sentences.n: “jemandem gute Worte geben” — to coax someone, to talk them round. “möchte” is subjunctive: that she should.

sentences.t: Da zog sie sich weiß an, und ihr Vater gab ihr einen Wagen mit sechs Pferden und herrliche Bedienten, Geld und Gut.
sentences.l: Then dressed she herself in white, and her father gave her a carriage with six horses and splendid servants, money and goods.
sentences.i: So she dressed herself in white, and her father gave her a carriage and six, splendid servants, money and goods.
sentences.n: “sich anziehen” — to dress oneself; “weiß” is the colour here, the white of a bride. A coach and six marks a princess travelling.

sentences.t: Sie setzte sich ein, und Hans mein Igel mit seinem Hahn und Dudelsack neben sie,
sentences.l: She set herself in, and Hans my Hedgehog with his cock and bagpipe beside her,
sentences.i: She took her seat, and Hans My Hedgehog beside her with his cock and bagpipe,
sentences.n: The verb is not repeated for Hans — German lets “setzte sich ein” carry over to him from the first half of the sentence. “sich einsetzen” — to seat oneself in the carriage (separable ein-).

sentences.t: dann nahmen sie Abschied und zogen fort, und der König dachte er kriegte sie nicht wieder zu sehen.
sentences.l: then took they leave and moved off, and the king thought he would not get to see her again.
sentences.i: then they took their leave and drove away, and the king thought he would never see her again.
sentences.n: “Abschied nehmen” — to take leave. “kriegte … zu sehen” — would get to see.

sentences.t: Es gieng aber anders als er dachte,
sentences.l: It went however otherwise than he thought,
sentences.i: But it went otherwise than he thought,
sentences.n: A flat narrator’s line at the turn of the tale; “anders als” — otherwise than.

sentences.t: denn als sie ein Stück Wegs von der Stadt waren, da zog ihr Hans mein Igel die schönen Kleider aus,
sentences.l: for when they were a stretch of road from the town, there pulled Hans my Hedgehog the beautiful clothes off her,
sentences.i: for when they were some way out of the town, Hans My Hedgehog stripped her fine clothes off her,
sentences.n: “ein Stück Wegs” keeps the old genitive: a piece of road. “ihr … ausziehen” — the person is in the dative: took the clothes off her.

sentences.t: und stach sie mit seiner Igelhaut bis sie ganz blutig war,
sentences.l: and pricked her with his hedgehog-skin until she was all bloody,
sentences.i: and pricked her with his hedgehog skin until she was all over blood,
sentences.n: The tale neither softens this nor explains it away, and the apparatus does not either: he strips and bloodies her for her father’s lie, not for anything she did. “Igelhaut” is the spiny hide he wears and later sheds. “stach” here is pricked, stabbed (stechen).

sentences.t: sagte „das ist der Lohn für eure Falschheit, geh hin, ich will dich nicht,“
sentences.l: said “that is the wage for your falseness, go away, I will not have you,”
sentences.i: and said, “That is the reward for your falseness — go your way, I will not have you,”
sentences.n: “Lohn” is wage or reward, said bitterly. He begins with the plural “eure”, your — the falseness is her father’s as much as hers — and turns to the singular “dich” to dismiss her.

sentences.t: und jagte sie damit nach Haus, und war sie beschimpft ihr Lebtag.
sentences.l: and chased her with that home, and was she disgraced all her days.
sentences.i: and with that he drove her home, and she was disgraced all her life.
sentences.n: “beschimpft” in older usage is put to shame, dishonoured — a lasting public disgrace, not merely insulted. “ihr Lebtag” — all her days.

sentences.t: Hans mein Igel aber ritt weiter auf seinem Göckelhahn und mit seinem Dudelsack nach dem zweiten Königreich, wo er dem König auch den Weg gezeigt hatte.
sentences.l: Hans my Hedgehog however rode on upon his cockerel and with his bagpipe to the second kingdom, where he had shown the king the way too.
sentences.i: But Hans My Hedgehog rode on, on his cockerel and with his bagpipe, to the second kingdom, where he had also shown the king the way.
sentences.n: “nach … reiten” — to ride to a place; the whole tale is built on the pair of kingdoms and their two receptions.

sentences.t: Der aber hatte bestellt, wenn einer käme, wie Hans mein Igel, sollten sie das Gewehr präsentieren, ihn frei hereinführen, Vivat rufen, und ihn ins königliche Schloß bringen.
sentences.l: That one however had given order, if anyone came like Hans my Hedgehog, they should present the musket, lead him in freely, call Vivat, and bring him into the royal castle.
sentences.i: But that king had given orders that if anyone came who was like Hans My Hedgehog, they should present arms, lead him in freely, cry Vivat, and bring him into the royal castle.
sentences.n: “Der” at the head is the demonstrative for the second king. “das Gewehr präsentieren” is the drill command, to present arms; “Vivat rufen” is the shout of “long live him” at a royal entry. Bayonets in one kingdom, a guard of honour in the other.

sentences.t: Wie ihn nun die Königstochter sah, war sie erschrocken, weil er doch gar zu wunderlich aussah,
sentences.l: When now the king’s daughter saw him, was she frightened, because he did look altogether too strange,
sentences.i: Now when the king’s daughter saw him she was frightened, for he did look far too strange,
sentences.n: “gar zu” — far too, altogether too. “doch” concedes the point: he really did.

sentences.t: sie dachte aber es wäre nicht anders, sie hätte es ihrem Vater versprochen.
sentences.l: but she thought it was not otherwise, she had promised it to her father.
sentences.i: but she thought there was no help for it: she had promised her father.
sentences.n: “es wäre nicht anders” — there is no other way, it cannot be helped.

sentences.t: Da ward Hans mein Igel von ihr bewillkommt, und ward mit ihr vermählt,
sentences.l: Then was Hans my Hedgehog welcomed by her, and was wedded to her,
sentences.i: So Hans My Hedgehog was welcomed by her and wedded to her,
sentences.n: “bewillkommt” is the older form of “bewillkommnet”, welcomed. “ward” is again the old preterite of werden, here as the passive auxiliary.

sentences.t: und er mußte mit an die königliche Tafel gehen, und sie setzte sich zu seiner Seite, und sie aßen und tranken.
sentences.l: and he had to go along to the royal table, and she set herself at his side, and they ate and drank.
sentences.i: and he had to go with them to the royal table, and she seated herself at his side, and they ate and drank.
sentences.n: “mit” alone stands for “mitgehen”, to go along. “Tafel” is the great formal table of a court, not any table.

sentences.t: Wies nun Abend ward, daß sie wollten schlafen gehen, da fürchtete sie sich sehr vor seinen Stacheln:
sentences.l: When it now became evening, so that they wanted to go to sleep, then was she very afraid of his spines:
sentences.i: When evening came and they were to go to bed, she was in great fear of his spines:
sentences.n: “Wies” is “wie es” run together. “sich fürchten vor” — to be afraid of, with the dative.

sentences.t: er aber sprach, sie sollte sich nicht fürchten, es geschähe ihr kein Leid,
sentences.l: he however spoke, she should not be afraid, no harm would happen to her,
sentences.i: but he said she should not be afraid; no harm would come to her,
sentences.n: “es geschähe ihr kein Leid” is impersonal, with the person in the dative: no harm should befall her. The subjunctive reports his promise.

sentences.t: und sagte zu dem alten König, er sollte vier Mann bestellen, die sollten wachen vor der Kammerthüre und ein großes Feuer anmachen,
sentences.l: and said to the old king, he should order four men, they should watch before the chamber door and light a great fire,
sentences.i: and told the old king to order four men, who should keep watch before the chamber door and light a great fire,
sentences.n: “vier Mann” keeps the singular after a numeral, as counting soldiers does. “Kammerthüre” is the 1857 spelling of Kammertüre, chamber door. “anmachen” — to light, to kindle.

sentences.t: und wann er in die Kammer eingienge und sich ins Bett legen wollte, würde er aus seiner Igelshaut herauskriechen und sie vor dem Bett liegen lassen:
sentences.l: and when he went into the chamber and wanted to lay himself in the bed, he would crawl out of his hedgehog-skin and let it lie before the bed:
sentences.i: and that when he went into the chamber and was ready to lie down in bed, he would crawl out of his hedgehog skin and leave it lying before the bed:
sentences.n: “wann” again for “wenn”. “eingienge” is the subjunctive of “eingehen”, to go in. “Igelshaut” carries a linking -s- where the same word stood without one earlier in the tale; both spellings are in the 1857 text and neither is corrected here.

sentences.t: dann sollten die Männer hurtig herbeispringen und sie ins Feuer werfen, auch dabei bleiben, bis sie vom Feuer verzehrt wäre.
sentences.l: then should the men spring up quickly and throw it into the fire, also stay by it, until it was consumed by the fire.
sentences.i: then the men should spring up quickly and throw it into the fire, and stay by it until the fire had consumed it.
sentences.n: “hurtig” — brisk, quick (old-fashioned). “dabei bleiben” — to stay by it: the skin has to be watched to the end, or the release fails.

sentences.t: Wie die Glocke nun elfe schlug, da gieng er in die Kammer, streifte die Igelshaut ab, und ließ sie vor dem Bette liegen:
sentences.l: When the clock now struck eleven, then went he into the chamber, stripped the hedgehog-skin off, and let it lie before the bed:
sentences.i: When the clock struck eleven he went into the chamber, stripped off the hedgehog skin, and left it lying before the bed:
sentences.n: “elfe” is the old form of “elf”, eleven; the hour matters, for the work is done before midnight. “abstreifen” — to strip off (separable: streifte … ab).

sentences.t: da kamen die Männer und holten sie geschwind und warfen sie ins Feuer;
sentences.l: then came the men and fetched it quickly and threw it into the fire;
sentences.i: then the men came and quickly fetched it and threw it into the fire;
sentences.n: “sie” is the skin, which is feminine in German (“die Haut”); English has to say “it”.

sentences.t: und als sie das Feuer verzehrt hatte, da war er erlöst, und lag da im Bett ganz als ein Mensch gestaltet, aber er war kohlschwarz wie gebrannt.
sentences.l: and when the fire had consumed it, then was he released, and lay there in the bed wholly shaped as a human being, but he was coal-black as if burnt.
sentences.i: and when the fire had consumed it he was released from the spell, and lay there in the bed formed wholly as a man, but coal-black, as though burnt.
sentences.n: “erlöst” — released, redeemed: the standing word for the breaking of an enchantment. “gestaltet” — shaped, formed.

sentences.t: Der König schickte zu seinem Arzt, der wusch ihn mit guten Salben und balsamirte ihn, da ward er weiß, und war ein schöner junger Herr.
sentences.l: The king sent to his physician, who washed him with good salves and anointed him, then became he white, and was a handsome young gentleman.
sentences.i: The king sent for his physician, who washed him with good salves and anointed him, and then he became white, and was a handsome young gentleman.
sentences.n: “balsamiren” (modern balsamieren) — to treat with balsam, to anoint. “weiß” is the colour again, set against the coal-black of the burning.

sentences.t: Wie das die Königstochter sah, war sie froh,
sentences.l: When the king’s daughter saw that, was she glad,
sentences.i: When the king’s daughter saw that, she was glad,
sentences.n: Her gladness comes only now, once the skin is burnt; before this she had nothing but her promise to her father.

sentences.t: und am andern Morgen stiegen sie mit Freuden auf, aßen und tranken,
sentences.l: and on the next morning rose they up with joy, ate and drank,
sentences.i: and next morning they rose up in joy, ate and drank,
sentences.n: “am andern Morgen” — on the next morning; “ander” in older usage often means simply “next”. “aufsteigen” here in the plain sense of getting up out of bed (separable: stiegen … auf).

sentences.t: und ward die Vermählung erst recht gefeiert, und Hans mein Igel bekam das Königreich von dem alten König.
sentences.l: and was the wedding only now properly celebrated, and Hans my Hedgehog got the kingdom from the old king.
sentences.i: and now the wedding was celebrated in earnest, and Hans My Hedgehog received the kingdom from the old king.
sentences.n: “erst recht” — now properly, in earnest: the first ceremony was got through, this one is kept.

sentences.t: Wie etliche Jahre herum waren, fuhr er mit seiner Gemahlin zu seinem Vater und sagte er wäre sein Sohn;
sentences.l: When some years were round, drove he with his consort to his father and said he was his son;
sentences.i: When some years had gone round he drove with his wife to his father and said that he was his son;
sentences.n: “herum sein”, of time — to be up, be over. “Gemahlin” is the formal word for a wife of rank.

sentences.t: der Vater aber sprach er hätte keinen, er hätte nur einen gehabt, der wäre aber wie ein Igel mit Stacheln geboren worden, und wäre in die Welt gegangen.
sentences.l: the father however spoke he had none, he had had only one, but he had been born like a hedgehog with spines, and had gone off into the world.
sentences.i: but the father said he had no son; he had had only one, but that one had been born like a hedgehog with spines and had gone off into the world.
sentences.n: Four subjunctives in a row — “hätte … hätte … wäre … wäre” — keep the whole speech reported. The father denies him even now, to his face.

sentences.t: Da gab er sich zu erkennen, und der alte Vater freute sich und gieng mit ihm in sein Königreich.
sentences.l: Then gave he himself to be recognized, and the old father rejoiced and went with him into his kingdom.
sentences.i: Then he made himself known, and the old father rejoiced and went with him into his kingdom.
sentences.n: “sich zu erkennen geben” — to make oneself known, to reveal who one is. The reconciliation gets one line and no explanation at all.

sentences.t:
Mein Märchen ist aus,
und geht vor Gustchen sein Haus.
sentences.l:
My tale is out,
and goes before Gustchen’s house.
sentences.i:
My tale is done,
and goes past little Gussie’s house.
sentences.n: A closing tag of the kind tellers used to hand the story on: the tale walks off down the street. “Gustchen sein Haus” is the everyday dative-possessive — “Gustchen his house” — where written German wants “Gustchens Haus”; Gustchen is a pet form of Auguste. “aus sein” — to be over, finished.

glossary.acht: acht — eight (the number; the noun die Acht, heed, is a different word)
glossary.drangen: eindringen — pressed in, assailed (3rd pl. past; separable ein-: drangen … ein)
glossary.elfe: elf — eleven (older form; die Glocke schlug elfe, the clock struck eleven)
glossary.es: es — it (neuter pronoun; also ‘he/she’ for neuter nouns such as das Kind, das Mädchen)
glossary.feder: die Feder — pen, quill (Feder und Dinte: pen and ink); also: feather
glossary.gedachte: gedenken — remembered, called to mind (3rd sg. past; here gedenken an + acc.)
glossary.hacken: hacken — hacking, chopping (infinitive used as a noun: ein Hacken)
glossary.hüte: hüten — tend, herd (1st sg. present, ich hüte); sich hüten: to beware
glossary.liebe: die Liebe — love (jemandem zu Liebe: for someone’s sake; the adjective lieb is dear)
glossary.liegen: liegen — to lie (infinitive; liegen lassen: to leave lying)
glossary.müde: müde — tired, weary (jemanden müde sein: to be tired of someone, with the accusative)
glossary.ordentlich: ordentlich — proper, orderly (adj., here uninflected before Bett); as adverb: properly
glossary.reit: reiten — ride (1st sg. present, reit ich = reite ich)
glossary.sollt: sollen — should (clipped for sollte, 3rd sg.; also 2nd pl. sollt)
glossary.streifte: abstreifen — stripped off (3rd sg. past; separable ab-: streifte … ab; streifen alone: to brush, graze)
glossary.wollt: wollen — wanted (clipped for wollte, 3rd sg. past; also 2nd pl. wollt)
glossary.zogen: fortziehen — moved off, set out (3rd pl. past; separable fort-; ziehen alone: to pull, to draw)
